title: The End Has Come
summary: In a breathless poem, God announces that the end has come upon the land of Israel. The day is near, and neither wealth, trade, weapons, prophets, priests, elders, nor king can stop it. Silver and gold will be thrown into the streets, the temple will be profaned by foreigners, and the people will be judged by their own standards so that they will know that he is the LORD.
story: This chapter closes the first major section of the book of Ezekiel (chapters 1 to 7), which runs from the prophet's call through the sign-acts of the siege to this final announcement. Chapter 6 addressed the mountains; chapter 7 addresses the land as a whole and declares that its time is up. The next section (chapters 8 to 11) will show why, by taking Ezekiel in a vision into the temple itself. For readers following the Bible as one story, this is the point where the long warnings of the prophets since Amos and Hosea reach their deadline. What was coming is now here.
historical:
The oracle is undated but belongs among the messages Ezekiel gave in Babylon between 593 BC and the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. At that time Judah still had a king (Zedekiah), a temple, priests, prophets, and elders, and many of the exiles, as well as the people still in Jerusalem, trusted that these institutions guaranteed the city's survival. Verse 26 names exactly these sources of guidance and says each will fail: the prophet's vision, the priest's instruction, the elders' counsel. Jeremiah, preaching in Jerusalem during the same years, fought the same confidence and records prophets who promised peace when there was none (Jeremiah 6:14; 28).

The details of the poem fit the reality of a Babylonian siege and conquest: fighting outside the walls, famine and disease within, survivors fleeing to the hills, the temple treasures carried away, and the king in mourning. According to 2 Kings 25, the Babylonians burned the temple, took its bronze, gold, and silver, and captured Zedekiah as he fled.
cultural:
Verses 12 and 13 assume the economy of a land-owning people. Under the Law of Moses, family land that had been sold was supposed to return to its owner in the year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25). A seller might grieve losing his field, and a buyer might rejoice at the gain, but Ezekiel says both reactions are pointless, because conquest will cancel every transaction. The buyer will not keep it, and the seller will not live to recover it.

The signs of mourning in verse 18 (sackcloth, a coarse cloth worn in grief, and shaved heads) were common across the ancient Near East. The picture of silver and gold thrown into the streets (verse 19) is striking because precious metal was the ancient world's ultimate security. The same metals had been used to make idols (verse 20), so they became a stumbling block twice over: they fed the people's pride, and they gave form to their false worship. The phrase “the day of the wrath of the LORD” draws on the prophetic theme of the Day of the LORD, which Amos, Isaiah, and Zephaniah had used for a coming day when God would act decisively in judgment.
literary: Chapter 7 is poetry, compressed and repetitive, meant to be heard as an alarm. The word “end” rings out five times in verses 2 to 6, and verses 3 and 4 are repeated almost word for word in verses 8 and 9, like a refrain. Short, clipped lines pile up: “The end has come,” “The time has come,” “the day is near.” The Hebrew includes wordplay that English cannot fully carry: in verse 6 the word for end (qets) sounds like the verb for awaking (quts), and the whole passage echoes Amos 8:2, where a basket of summer fruit (qayits) became a sign that the end (qets) had come for the northern kingdom. The chapter moves from the land (verses 1 to 9), to the day itself (verses 10 to 13), to the collapse of the city's defenses and wealth (verses 14 to 22), and finally to the collapse of its leadership (verses 23 to 27).

outline.t: The end has come upon the four corners of the land
Disaster upon disaster: the refrain repeated
The day has arrived: buying and selling made meaningless
No one goes to war: sword, plague, and famine
Silver, gold, and the treasured place defiled
A chain for the violent city, and leaders who fail

doctrines.note: Judgment here is according to “your ways” (verses 3, 4, 8, 9, 27). God judges people by the standards they themselves have lived by, so that judgment reveals what was already there rather than imposing something foreign.

The end comes because God brings it. Kings, armies, wealth, and religious institutions cannot delay it. History is not a random series of events but is under the rule of the God who speaks through his prophets.

Verses 19 and 20 connect wealth and idolatry: silver and gold, meant as gifts, became both a source of pride and the raw material of idols. What people trust in place of God cannot save them in the day of trouble.

words.note: Qets, end. The word can mean the edge or limit of something, or the end of a period of time. In chapter 7 it means the end of Israel's life in the land as it had been known. Later biblical writers, especially the book of Daniel, use the same word for the time of the end.

Yom, day. Here the word carries the weight of the prophetic Day of the LORD: not an ordinary day but a moment of divine intervention. Earlier prophets warned that Israel's hope for that day would turn to dread if they were unfaithful (Amos 5:18-20).

Chamas, violence. It refers to injustice and cruelty, often by the powerful against the weak. In verse 23 the city is “full of violence.” Ezekiel does not only accuse Jerusalem of false worship but of social wrongdoing and bloodshed, and he treats the two as bound together.

Torah, instruction or law. In verse 26 it is the guidance priests were expected to give from God's law. The word is broader than a legal code: it means teaching that shows the way to live. Its failing is one sign of the end, since the people no longer have anyone to direct them.

christ: The Day of the LORD announced here is a pattern the New Testament picks up. Jesus spoke of a coming day when Jerusalem would again be surrounded and its temple destroyed (Luke 21:20-24), which happened in AD 70, and of a final day of judgment for all nations. The apostles took the Day of the LORD and applied it to the day of Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). At the same time, the Gospels present the cross as the place where judgment fell on Jesus, and Paul can speak of believers being rescued from the coming wrath through him (1 Thessalonians 1:10). This connection is thematic: Ezekiel's words are about Jerusalem in the sixth century BC, and the New Testament sees in them a pattern that runs to the end of history.
questions: The people trusted their temple, their prophets, and their wealth to keep them safe. What institutions or resources are you tempted to trust as guarantees?
Verse 27 says God will judge people “by their own standards.” What would it look like for you to be judged by the standards you apply to others?
How does it change the way you hold money and possessions to picture silver and gold thrown into the streets as worthless?
